facts.title: Slow down
facts.body: The single best defence against misinformation is a pause. Content designed to make you angry, scared, or certain is designed to be shared fast. If something makes you feel a strong emotion instantly, that's exactly the moment to stop and check before you react.

facts.title: Who is saying it?
facts.body: Look at who published the claim before you look at whether you agree with it. Is it a news outlet with a corrections policy? A random account with no history? An anonymous screenshot with no link? The source matters more than the claim.

facts.title: Reverse-image search
facts.body: Right-click any image and use Google Lens, or upload it to TinEye. You'll often find the same photo used years ago in a completely different context. A picture of a protest, a flood, or a crowd is frequently recycled from another country and another year.

facts.title: Check the date
facts.body: Old photos and old videos get recycled constantly. A clip from a 2015 event can be posted today with a caption about a current crisis and look completely convincing. Search for the exact wording of the caption plus a keyword, and see if the story is actually new.

facts.title: There's something else
facts.body: You've probably noticed that nothing in this game talks about what happens when a false rumour spreads far enough. There's a longer story — a set of torn notes scattered through the levels. You'll start finding them as you go. Read them carefully. They're real.

facts.title: Search the exact quote
facts.body: If a post attributes a quote to a famous person, paste the quote into a search engine in quotation marks. If the only sources are other social media posts, the quote is probably fake. Real quotes are almost always reported by established outlets somewhere.

facts.title: Cropping changes meaning
facts.body: You don't need Photoshop to mislead. Crop a photo of a large, peaceful crowd down to three people and it looks like a small angry mob. Crop a wider shot down to a single moment and a polite exchange looks like a confrontation. The image is real; the framing isn't.

facts.title: Flipping and mirroring
facts.body: Some of the most effective fake photos are simply the real thing flipped horizontally. A face on the left becomes a face on the right, a sign becomes unreadable, and reverse-image searches struggle to match. Look for reversed text or asymmetrical landmarks as a clue.

facts.title: Headlines don't have to match the article
facts.body: A headline is written to get the click, not to summarise. Read past it. It's common for a headline to make a claim the article itself softens or contradicts in the second paragraph. Sharing the headline without reading the piece is one of the most common ways misinformation spreads.

facts.title: Screenshots are the easiest thing to fake
facts.body: A screenshot of a tweet, a text, or a headline can be made in ten seconds with browser developer tools or a template. Never trust a screenshot as evidence. Search for the original post. If it doesn't exist, it probably never did.

facts.title: The 'forwarded' label
facts.body: WhatsApp and other messaging apps mark messages that have been forwarded many times. That label is a warning sign, not a badge of authenticity. If five people already forwarded it to you before you read it, ask why. Chain messages are the oldest misinformation format there is.

facts.title: Misinformation vs. disinformation
facts.body: Misinformation is false information shared without intent to harm — someone believed it and passed it on. Disinformation is false information shared on purpose to deceive. Both cause the same damage. The trick is that most of what you'll encounter is misinformation, spread by people who honestly think they're helping.

facts.title: Fake grassroots movements
facts.body: Sometimes a hashtag or campaign looks like it's coming from thousands of ordinary people, but it's actually coordinated by a small group using many accounts. Look for identical phrasing across many posts, accounts created on the same day, or engagement that spikes and dies in minutes. Real movements build slowly.

facts.title: The habit is the point
facts.body: You will not catch every piece of misinformation. No one does. The goal is not to be immune — it's to build the habit of pausing, checking, and being willing to change your mind when the evidence says so. That willingness is the whole skill. That's what fact-checking actually is.
